REGENESIS EXPOSED: FREE STATE HEALTH

By: Este de Klerk | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Another controversial contract between the Free State Health Department and a service provider worth a max of R90 million for stem cell treatment, cancelled.

Unique Selling Point:
Carte Blanche has been investigating healthcare in the Free State health department for more than three years. During those three years, we have uncovered widespread maladministration in healthcare in the Free State province. It was during a follow-up investigation that a contract between the FS Health Department and a company owned by a dr Wian Stander called Regenesis Biotechnologies was leaked to us. The contract states that Dr Stander was appointed to provide "cell based stem cell therapies for muscoskeletal diseases such as shoulder, knee and hip replacements, autoimmune diseases and other burdensome diseases AND therapeutic research. The contract is worth a maximum of R90 million over three years and the service provider will receive an amount not exceeding R30 000 per treatment per patient. The department also guarantees a thousand patients per year.

Summary:
The National Health Department heard that we were investigating the contract and gave us a call because Health Minister, dr Aaron Motsoaledi was alarmed. We subsequently spoke to the Medicines Control Council who said that the Minister of Health immediately informed them and they sent two investigators immediately to go to the Regenesis Biotechnologies unit where dr Stander was treating patients with therapies including stem cell therapy. Dr Stander granted us an interview on the Monday, following the visit from the two MCC investigators. Dr Stander said the National Health Department was aware of the contract and what he was doing there and they have in fact visited the unit three days before and they've done an audit and investigation and all their findings were positive and they are in fact going to motivate to the provincial health department that he needed a larger space and larger theatre space because they could also see that the patients deserve it.
But Prof Rees said the two investigators went there to investigate, they interviewed dr Stander whom he thinks, did not appreciate the fact that what he was doing there was in fact a clinical trial and that the therapy he was treating patients with is in fact regarded as a medicine and both of those fall under the Medicines Control Council and he had permission to do neither.
Prof Rees said that dr Stander has never applied with the MCC to do any clinical trial, or to treat patients with muscoskeletal diseases with therapies including stem cell therapy.
Stem cell therapy can only be used in blood-related diseases, such as leukemia, bone marrow transplants etc. - that is regarded as standard care because clinical trials to prove the success of the treatment had been done worldwide. No clinical trial have been done to prove the risks, pros and cons of stem cell treatment on muscoskeletal diseases and it is not regarded as standard care in SA. Dr Stander insisted he didn't need approval from the MCC.

Further information:
Three days after the MCC investigators visited Dr Stander's Regenesis Biotechnologies's unit at Pelenomi Hospital, they handed in a report and the MCC instructed Dr Stander to immediately stop treating patients. The MCC has also informed the Free State Health Department that Dr Stander was in fact treating patients illegally because he had no permission from the MCC or any ethics committee to treat patients with those diseases with therapies including stem cell therapy and that what he was doing at Pelenomi Hospital could only be regarded as a clinical trial and Dr Stander had permission to do neither.

On the same day that the MCC instructed Dr Stander to immediately stop treating patients, the Free State Health Department cancelled his contract.
In our interview with the Free State Health Department, HOD, dr David Motau admitted that the department cancelled the contract because starting the contract in the first place was a mistake.

Script:


REGENESIS SCRIPT

PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK

PRESENTER: DEVI SANKAREE GOVDENDER

EDITOR: JAMES CARROLL

BROADCAST DATE: 2 OCTOBER 2016

[DR WIAN STANDER VIDEO ABOUT HIS SLIMMING CLINIC]
DR WIAN STANDER: I’m dr. Wian Stander. I qualified as a medical doctor from the University of Pretoria in ’99, I did a post-graduate qualification in anti-aging medicine and functional medicine.

Aside from owning slimming clinics, dr. Wian Stander also lists among his qualifications fellowships in anti-aging, functional and integrative medicine medicine and stem cell and cell-based therapies. Online he calls himself “a stem cell innovator”.
In June, he also became the head of a controversial unit at Pelenomi Hospital - the Free State’s largest provincial hospital – where patients are treated using stem cells harvested from their own bodies.

DEVI LINK: Stem cell therapy is used legally, locally and internationally with varying degrees of success in the treatment of blood-related cancers and diseases. But here at Pelenomi Hospital in Bloemfontein, patients with joint related and auto immune diseases are being treated with therapies, including stem cell therapy, but this is being done without approval from the MCC – that is the Medicines Control Council and the National Research Ethics Committee.

And at the head of this unit at Pelenomi is Dr. Stander – this time under one of his other companies, ReGenesis Bio-Technologies.
A tender was advertised by the Free State Health Department in April - seeking a service provider who can provide “cell based stem cell regenerative medicine and therapeutic research services”. Dr Stander was awarded the contract.

DR WIAN STANDER: Regenegesis Biotechnologies is a bio-medical facility where we are busy with translational medicine – that basically says we are taking the best from a scientifically proven world and we are translating that back to therapies for patients, and especially patients living with chronic degenerative diseases and patients living in chronic pain.

But something didn’t add up.
Stem cell therapy administered at a state hospital to treat joint-related and autoimmune diseases and not even the Minister of Health makes mention of it?

02:00 – 02:45 Over the last three years, Carte Blanche has uncovered wide-spread mal-administration in healthcare throughout the Free State province and it was during a follow-up investigation, that we were sent the service agreement between dr Stander’s company and the department.

While we were investigating we received a call from the National Department of Health. They’d heard about our enquiries, and Minister of Health, dr Aaron Motsoaledi was alarmed.

MINISTER OF HEALTH: You can’t, in a population of 54 million, allow any medicine whatsoever to be used among people, because you know what the results might be and so whenever we hear that there is something that is being done about a medicine which we don’t know to have been registered, obiviously we get very scared and we have got to become very, very swift.

And action was swift indeed.
Hours after the National Health department had been informed about the contract last Thursday, they started their own investigation and informed the Medicines Control Council’s chairperson, professor Helen Rees.

PROF. HELEN REES: Within 24 hours the inspectors from the MCC had visited the clinic, had produced a report within three days which we acted on, we asked for a lot of information, and we also instructed Dr Stander, given the mandate of the MCC, to stop treating patients immediately.

That was on Tuesday.
The day before dr. Stander gave us a different version.

DR. STANDER: The National Health Department is aware of our project, they actually as a matter of fact visited our unit three days ago and they did an audit and an inspection, all with positive findings. They are actually busy motivating to the local provincial health department just for larger premises and bigger theatre space because they the patients deserve it.

PROF. HELEN REES: They interviewed dr Stander, who didn’t appreciate, I think that what he was doing was clinical research, nor did he appreciate that the therapies that he was offering and that he was getting consent for to give to other patients was the use of the medicine and both of those fall under the Medicines Control Council and he had permission to do neither.

DR STANDER: Stander: Either a small piece of fat is harvested under local anesthetic procedure, so the patient is fully awake during this procedure, or the bone marrow aspiration and then from there it goes to a cell process in unit where the cell biologist and the scientific officer takes that sample and she extracts the growth factors and the stem cells from that sample where after we re-introduce it back into the patient’s body, either in the joint or intravenously.

PROF. HELEN REES: We don’t know how these stem cells are being removed, how they are being processed, they are said to be concentrated, where they are being stored, how they are re-administered, where they are re-administered to and there are many things along that line that could be of real safety concern to patients.

DR. TERRENCE CARTER: At the moment, stem cell therapy standard of care only applies to various hematological conditions, such as leukemia, lymphoma and so on.

Dr. Terrence Carter is the National Health Department’s deputy-director general for hospitals.

DR. TERRENCE CARTER: In the public sector stem cell treatment could possibly be used, but only in a research environment

PROF HELEN REES: But we have never received an application for a clinical trial and in the limited documentation that we have seen there is a specific reference to a therapeutic research and there is an informed consent that the patients have to sign which includes the possibility that their stem cells could be used in other patients. Now, for us this is experimentation.

DR STANDER: Currently we are just doing patient therapies and treatments, so the research arm, I think, is still a little while away, so there are a couple of committee’s that we first have to approach, but currently we are just doing patient treatments and we are validating the treatments with blood results and with clinical imagining, either MRI and CT scans.

After the MCC instructed dr Stander to stop treatment on Tuesday, he responded in writing to further Carte Blanche questions, saying he is acting in according with the National Health Act. He also insists that he is not conducting a clinical trial and as a result doesn’t need approval from the MCC.

PROF REES: Without the safety oversight of either properly registered medicines or a clinical trial, harm and safety is always a great concern.

So, how did this project become a reality?
The Free State Health Department’s MEC, dr Benny Malakoane and HOD, dr. David Motau are medical practitioners.
The HOD even surprised us with his decision.

DR. DAVID MOTAU: I cancelled the contract.

DEVI: Cancelled, postponed, put on hold, just so that we are clear?

DR. DAVID MOTAU: Cancelled.

DEVI: You should have gone to the MCC first and you should have gone to the National Research Ethics Committee?

DR. DAVID MOTAU: This department had already started to make sure that all those boxes are ticked. Through the department of orthopaedics, we had already engaged the service provider to say to him this is a list of things you need to submit and that is why I am saying now there is no, there is no need for us to continue, we have cancelled it and…

DEVI: No, you are not going to get away that easily, you are not going to get away that easily. So, if there were boxes that needed to be ticked and he didn’t tick it, then why did you allow him to continue with this form of therapy?

DR. DAVID MOTAU: Remember, I am saying to you – and now you dragging me to go into the details which I ….

DEVI: I’m not dragging you. You walked into it.

And did the department properly review dr Stander’s credentials?
Dr. Stander told Carte Blanche he was co-founder of the South African Stem Cell Institute and worked there.
But the Institute denies both claims and added Stander used their facilities for seven months to treat 15 of his patients with stem cell therapy.

DEVI: Were you aware when you first heard about the Regenesis unit, that because it hadn’t gone through the necessary protocols from a research point of view, that the question of whether patients’ lives were put at risk, was always there and unanswered?

DR. DAVID MOTAU: Which is the reason why we cancelled it.

DEVI: But you only cancelled it after the MCC, you see, if you had cancelled it before the MCC’s visit, I will shake your hand now.

DR. DAVID MOTAU: Already, already, the process of moving towards the cancellation was there.

DEVI: Too slow though.

For a cash-strapped department under administration, they sure had money for this venture. The Regenesis contract was worth a maximum of R90 million over three years.

According to the contract, the department “guarantees a thousand patients per annum and dr. Stander would be paid a claim per patient not exceeding R30 000 per treatment for the full service offering”.

DR. CARTER: The cost to the patient should have been, or even to the department, would have been zero. Because in fact, in developing any new modality of treatment, the research and development part is expensive and the bares the cost.

DEVI: If you are cash-strapped as it is, why then would you get involved in Regenesis which is currently described as experimental treatment? Why put the money there when you can actually hire more orthopedic surgeons, more anesthetists and resolve the issue like that, practically?

DR. DAVID MOTAU: The answer to that is that I have cancelled the contract. And I have said it to you before and whatever money that there is, is going to be used of course to do all those things because this, for me, is not going to work.

The MCC’s investigation into dr. Stander should be concluded soon.

DR. DAVID MOTAU: The reason we cancelled is because we realized that it was a bad decision.




PROMO’S

PROMO 1:10”

A controversial stem cell unit set up at a cash-strapped Free state Hospital.

REES: It appears there was also no permission from an ethics committee.



PROMO 2: 15”:

While investigating the crumbling healthcare in the Free State, we uncover controversial regenerative clinic where patients are treated with stem cells without ethical approval.

REES: it was experimental medicine

PROMO 3: 15”

DR STANDER: (the soundup we cut out: where he says: I am a regenerative medicine speciliast.

Our investigation into the Free State Health Department unearths a peculiar contract worth millions.

DR MOTAU: it was a bad decision.

Stem cell therapy administered at a state hospital to treat joint-related and autoimmune diseases and not even the Minister of Health makes mention of it? 02:00 – 02:45 Over the last three years, Carte Blanche has uncovered wide-spread mal-administration in healthcare throughout the Free State province and it was during a follow-up investigation, that we were sent the service agreement between dr Stander’s company and the department. While we were investigating we received a call from the National Department of Health. They’d heard about our enquiries, and Minister of Health, dr Aaron Motsoaledi was alarmed. MINISTER OF HEALTH: You can’t, in a population of 54 million, allow any medicine whatsoever to be used among people, because you know what the results might be and so whenever we hear that there is something that is being done about a medicine which we don’t know to have been registered, obiviously we get very scared and we have got to become very, very swift. And action was swift indeed. Hours after the National Health department had been informed about the contract last Thursday, they started their own investigation and informed the Medicines Control Council’s chairperson, professor Helen Rees. PROF. HELEN REES: Within 24 hours the inspectors from the MCC had visited the clinic, had produced a report within three days which we acted on, we asked for a lot of information, and we also instructed Dr Stander, given the mandate of the MCC, to stop treating patients immediately. That was on Tuesday. The day before dr. Stander gave us a different version. DR. STANDER: The National Health Department is aware of our project, they actually as a matter of fact visited our unit three days ago and they did an audit and an inspection, all with positive findings. They are actually busy motivating to the local provincial health department just for larger premises and bigger theatre space because they the patients deserve it. PROF. HELEN REES: They interviewed dr Stander, who didn’t appreciate, I think that what he was doing was clinical research, nor did he appreciate that the therapies that he was offering and that he was getting consent for to give to other patients was the use of the medicine and both of those fall under the Medicines Control Council and he had permission to do neither. DR STANDER: Stander: Either a small piece of fat is harvested under local anesthetic procedure, so the patient is fully awake during this procedure, or the bone marrow aspiration and then from there it goes to a cell process in unit where the cell biologist and the scientific officer takes that sample and she extracts the growth factors and the stem cells from that sample where after we re-introduce it back into the patient’s body, either in the joint or intravenously. PROF. HELEN REES: We don’t know how these stem cells are being removed, how they are being processed, they are said to be concentrated, where they are being stored, how they are re-administered, where they are re-administered to and there are many things along that line that could be of real safety concern to patients. DR. TERRENCE CARTER: At the moment, stem cell therapy standard of care only applies to various hematological conditions, such as leukemia, lymphoma and so on. Dr. Terrence Carter is the National Health Department’s deputy-director general for hospitals. DR. TERRENCE CARTER: In the public sector stem cell treatment could possibly be used, but only in a research environment PROF HELEN REES: But we have never received an application for a clinical trial and in the limited documentation that we have seen there is a specific reference to a therapeutic research and there is an informed consent that the patients have to sign which includes the possibility that their stem cells could be used in other patients. Now, for us this is experimentation. DR STANDER: Currently we are just doing patient therapies and treatments, so the research arm, I think, is still a little while away, so there are a couple of committee’s that we first have to approach, but currently we are just doing patient treatments and we are validating the treatments with blood results and with clinical imagining, either MRI and CT scans. After the MCC instructed dr Stander to stop treatment on Tuesday, he responded in writing to further Carte Blanche questions, saying he is acting in according with the National Health Act. He also insists that he is not conducting a clinical trial and as a result doesn’t need approval from the MCC. PROF REES: Without the safety oversight of either properly registered medicines or a clinical trial, harm and safety is always a great concern. So, how did this project become a reality? The Free State Health Department’s MEC, dr Benny Malakoane and HOD, dr. David Motau are medical practitioners. The HOD even surprised us with his decision. DR. DAVID MOTAU: I cancelled the contract. DEVI: Cancelled, postponed, put on hold, just so that we are clear? DR. DAVID MOTAU: Cancelled. DEVI: You should have gone to the MCC first and you should have gone to the National Research Ethics Committee? DR. DAVID MOTAU: This department had already started to make sure that all those boxes are ticked. Through the department of orthopaedics, we had already engaged the service provider to say to him this is a list of things you need to submit and that is why I am saying now there is no, there is no need for us to continue, we have cancelled it and… DEVI: No, you are not going to get away that easily, you are not going to get away that easily. So, if there were boxes that needed to be ticked and he didn’t tick it, then why did you allow him to continue with this form of therapy? DR. DAVID MOTAU: Remember, I am saying to you – and now you dragging me to go into the details which I …. DEVI: I’m not dragging you. You walked into it. And did the department properly review dr Stander’s credentials? Dr. Stander told Carte Blanche he was co-founder of the South African Stem Cell Institute and worked there. But the Institute denies both claims and added Stander used their facilities for seven months to treat 15 of his patients with stem cell therapy. DEVI: Were you aware when you first heard about the Regenesis unit, that because it hadn’t gone through the necessary protocols from a research point of view, that the question of whether patients’ lives were put at risk, was always there and unanswered? DR. DAVID MOTAU: Which is the reason why we cancelled it. DEVI: But you only cancelled it after the MCC, you see, if you had cancelled it before the MCC’s visit, I will shake your hand now. DR. DAVID MOTAU: Already, already, the process of moving towards the cancellation was there. DEVI: Too slow though. For a cash-strapped department under administration, they sure had money for this venture. The Regenesis contract was worth a maximum of R90 million over three years. According to the contract, the department “guarantees a thousand patients per annum and dr. Stander would be paid a claim per patient not exceeding R30 000 per treatment for the full service offering”. DR. CARTER: The cost to the patient should have been, or even to the department, would have been zero. Because in fact, in developing any new modality of treatment, the research and development part is expensive and the bares the cost. DEVI: If you are cash-strapped as it is, why then would you get involved in Regenesis which is currently described as experimental treatment? Why put the money there when you can actually hire more orthopedic surgeons, more anesthetists and resolve the issue like that, practically? DR. DAVID MOTAU: The answer to that is that I have cancelled the contract. And I have said it to you before and whatever money that there is, is going to be used of course to do all those things because this, for me, is not going to work. The MCC’s investigation into dr. Stander should be concluded soon. DR. DAVID MOTAU: The reason we cancelled is because we realized that it was a bad decision. PROMO’S PROMO 1:10” A controversial stem cell unit set up at a cash-strapped Free state Hospital. REES: It appears there was also no permission from an ethics committee. PROMO 2: 15”: While investigating the crumbling healthcare in the Free State, we uncover controversial regenerative clinic where patients are treated with stem cells without ethical approval. REES: it was experimental medicine PROMO 3: 15” DR STANDER: (the soundup we cut out: where he says: I am a regenerative medicine speciliast. Our investigation into the Free State Health Department unearths a peculiar contract worth millions. DR MOTAU: it was a bad decision.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Another controversial contract between the Free State Health Department and a service provider worth a max of R90 million for stem cell treatment, cancelled.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Carte Blanche has been investigating healthcare in the Free State health department for more than three years. During those three years, we have uncovered widespread maladministration in healthcare in the Free State province. It was during a follow-up investigation that a contract between the FS Health Department and a company owned by a dr Wian Stander called Regenesis Biotechnologies was leaked to us. The contract states that Dr Stander was appointed to provide "cell based stem cell therapies for muscoskeletal diseases such as shoulder, knee and hip replacements, autoimmune diseases and other burdensome diseases AND therapeutic research. The contract is worth a maximum of R90 million over three years and the service provider will receive an amount not exceeding R30 000 per treatment per patient. The department also guarantees a thousand patients per year.
metadata.Summary: The National Health Department heard that we were investigating the contract and gave us a call because Health Minister, dr Aaron Motsoaledi was alarmed. We subsequently spoke to the Medicines Control Council who said that the Minister of Health immediately informed them and they sent two investigators immediately to go to the Regenesis Biotechnologies unit where dr Stander was treating patients with therapies including stem cell therapy. Dr Stander granted us an interview on the Monday, following the visit from the two MCC investigators. Dr Stander said the National Health Department was aware of the contract and what he was doing there and they have in fact visited the unit three days before and they've done an audit and investigation and all their findings were positive and they are in fact going to motivate to the provincial health department that he needed a larger space and larger theatre space because they could also see that the patients deserve it. But Prof Rees said the two investigators went there to investigate, they interviewed dr Stander whom he thinks, did not appreciate the fact that what he was doing there was in fact a clinical trial and that the therapy he was treating patients with is in fact regarded as a medicine and both of those fall under the Medicines Control Council and he had permission to do neither. Prof Rees said that dr Stander has never applied with the MCC to do any clinical trial, or to treat patients with muscoskeletal diseases with therapies including stem cell therapy. Stem cell therapy can only be used in blood-related diseases, such as leukemia, bone marrow transplants etc. - that is regarded as standard care because clinical trials to prove the success of the treatment had been done worldwide. No clinical trial have been done to prove the risks, pros and cons of stem cell treatment on muscoskeletal diseases and it is not regarded as standard care in SA. Dr Stander insisted he didn't need approval from the MCC.
metadata.Further information: Three days after the MCC investigators visited Dr Stander's Regenesis Biotechnologies's unit at Pelenomi Hospital, they handed in a report and the MCC instructed Dr Stander to immediately stop treating patients. The MCC has also informed the Free State Health Department that Dr Stander was in fact treating patients illegally because he had no permission from the MCC or any ethics committee to treat patients with those diseases with therapies including stem cell therapy and that what he was doing at Pelenomi Hospital could only be regarded as a clinical trial and Dr Stander had permission to do neither. On the same day that the MCC instructed Dr Stander to immediately stop treating patients, the Free State Health Department cancelled his contract. In our interview with the Free State Health Department, HOD, dr David Motau admitted that the department cancelled the contract because starting the contract in the first place was a mistake.
